title: Midnight Phone Vigils for Ghosts: Millions of Foreign Users Pay for AI-Powered Ghost Hunting Memberships
excerpt: In recent years, an increasing number of international paranormal enthusiasts and research teams have leveraged cutting-edge artificial intelligence technologies to conduct systematic ghost-hunting investigations, marking a groundbreaking shift from traditional subjective paranormal detection methods to data-driven, precision-focused exploration. By integrating AI-powered anomaly recognition algorithms, intelligent audio signal processing, computer vision for subtle environmental change tracking, and real-time multi-sensor data fusion systems, these foreign AI-assisted ghost hunting practices can accurately capture previously undetectable faint paranormal traces, analyze ambiguous voice recordings and blurry visual evidence with unprecedented efficiency, and leave alleged supernatural entities "nowhere to hide". This emerging cross-field application has not only sparked widespread global discussions on the boundaries between paranormal research and technological innovation, but also drawn attention from tech communities to the unconventional use scenarios of AI in uncharted exploration fields.
content:
There is an unbreakable rule known to all:

The moment humans get any new technology, they will immediately use it for adult content-related purposes.

But there is another group of people who are no slower than them in pursuing new technologies, and that is the paranormal investigation community.

As soon as a new gadget comes out, it won't be long before someone carries it around to hunt for ghosts.

In ancient times, people had Zhong Kui and yellow talismans, which relied on handcraft skills, but later the work became technology-driven.

After radios became popular, some people waved their radios to scan back and forth across channels, insisting that there were ghost cries in the noise and that they were tuning into the afterlife radio station. As soon as cameras were invented, a translucent shadow appeared in a photo, and everyone pointed at it and said it must be that "thing".

Today, it is AI's turn to bring technological upgrades to this old craft.

Recently, an app has suddenly become a hit in the overseas paranormal investigation community, called GhostTube SEER, which claims to be "the world's first AI ghost-hunting tool".

What it does sounds quite absurd: you stand in a "haunted house" and ask what happened here before. After a while, an image pops up on the screen: a woman, an old house...

You ask questions to the air, and it outputs an image from time to time, making you feel like there is really some "thing" responding to you. Doing this at midnight is extremely thrilling, and its downloads on the Google Play Store have exceeded 1 million.

There are far more people holding their phones at midnight waiting for ghosts to manifest than you can imagine.

01 Open a ghost-hunting app at midnight

Imagine it is midnight now, you are standing alone in the corridor of an old house, with all the lights off.

You take out your phone, open SEER, the screen goes black for a few seconds first, and it is so quiet that you can hear yourself swallowing.

The screen lights up, showing the corridor captured by the phone, covered with a dark filter, the atmosphere is perfectly set, you are in the right place. There is a magnetic field indicator on the screen, which is said to show the magnetic field changes in the house. This is part of paranormal investigation lore: when a ghost comes, it will disturb the surrounding magnetic field, but for now it is still very stable.

You whisper: Is there anyone here?

Nothing happens, you let out a sigh of relief, but feel a little disappointed at the same time.

You move a few steps towards the end of the corridor, stop in front of a closed door, the magnetic field jolts suddenly, and your scalp tingles immediately.

In the middle of the screen, an image slowly emerges: a woman standing in front of a window.

It turns out that the "thing" in the room wanted to show you something through the change of magnetic field.

You can keep asking, keep walking, and it will show you a new "thing" from time to time. You can also save the images to your photo album, or record them as videos to watch slowly later.

Of course, playing casually in an ordinary old house is not fun enough. If you want to have a great experience, just go all out, just like the developer of this app, and directly open it in a haunted mansion.

The creators of SEER are an Australian couple, Amy and Jarrad.

Their full-time job is shooting paranormal investigation videos, they go to stay overnight wherever is famous for being haunted, the kind of people who treat haunted houses like homestays. In one episode, they went to the Winchester Mystery House in California.

This mansion is one of the most famous haunted houses in the United States. Legend has it that after the hostess's husband and daughter passed away one after another, a medium told her that the wronged souls killed by Winchester rifles were haunting her. As long as the house kept being built, the wronged souls could not get close to her.

So this house was built day and night, expanding from 8 rooms to about 160 rooms. There are doors that lead nowhere, stairs that go nowhere, the number 13 appears repeatedly in the house, the whole house is a large custom-built maze for ghosts. No one can tell exactly what happened there, and everyone has their own version of the legend.

Photo | There is a "door to the void" on the outer wall of the Winchester Mystery House

The two of them sat down in a room in the mansion, opened the app, and Jarrad asked the air: "Can you show us what happened in this room before?"

A wooden wall with golden curtains hanging on it first appeared on the screen, looking like an old-fashioned bedroom.

After a while, an image of a woman reading a book popped up.

Then came a woman wearing a black shawl.

Finally, a group of white birds flying up appeared.

In a house that a widow built for decades to avoid ghosts, a woman wearing a black shawl showed up. If I were sitting there, my back would have already turned cold.

What their audience loves most is moments like this. A long-time follower who has watched all their videos said what gave her the most goosebumps was that the corridors and rooms generated by the app matched the place where the two of them were staying at that time.

When you "catch" a ghost, you definitely want to show it off, and it's even better if you can comment on it. There is a community in the app, where everyone posts the images they captured in different places, to watch and comment on each other. The community also collects more than 1000 haunted locations around the world. If you want to go paranormal investigation on weekends, you can first check what others have captured there, which is like the paranormal investigation version of review platforms.

You can't meet a ghost whenever you want. Free users have a daily limit on how many ghosts they can see. If you want ghosts to appear more often, you need to get a membership, which costs $3.99 per month and $14.99 per year.

How often ghosts appear depends on whether you pay the money. This is probably the most cyber, post-modern, and consumerist paranormal setting I have ever seen.

This setting has attracted the most senior veteran paranormal investigators to this app. It's hard to imagine what their customer service has to face every day. An old user who claims to be a born medium had his annual fee deducted normally but his account restricted, he was so angry that he cursed in the comment section, and finally dropped a harsh word, roughly meaning: You have angered the spirits. It's like summoning ghosts on the spot and fighting magic with magic.

Audio and images are not enough to satisfy them. The couple also sells a head-mounted display called GhostTube Lens, which follows the same idea as cheap mobile VR headsets: insert your phone into it, put it on your face, and there is only a screen in front of you, with total darkness all around.

Put it on, and your "third eye" is opened.

After putting it on, you can choose something to stare at: smoke, flames, a swinging pendulum clock, or full-screen static noise. For those who choose static noise, anyone who has watched *Ringu* knows that according to the plot, someone should crawl out of the screen in the next second.

This way of wearing it is well-founded. There is an old method in the paranormal investigation community: one person covers their eyes and wears noise-canceling headphones to isolate the senses of the real world as much as possible, then another person asks questions beside them, and the blindfolded person shouts out whatever they hear.

They believe that when your eyes and ears are blocked, your perception of "the other side" will be more sensitive. Now the eye mask is replaced by a screen, and what the ghost wants to say will appear in front of your eyes.

The good news is that buying the head-mounted display in the app also comes with a one-year membership.

The couple has made five ghost-hunting apps one after another, with downloads often exceeding millions. They have turned ghost-hunting into a complete product suite.

02 Cyber ghost-hunting guide

At this point, some people may be curious: ghosts are so mysterious, how on earth are they "seen" by the app?

It's no secret that if you take SEER apart, the whole process from a ghost being generated to appearing on your screen only has three steps: scan the magnetic field, draw a random word, and turn the word into an image. It's so simple that you almost want to ask for a refund.

SEER can respond thanks to a small chip called magnetometer in the phone. Almost every phone has one, and its original job is to measure the strength and direction of the surrounding magnetic field, so that map apps can know which direction you are facing.

The problem is that we all know a law: where there is electric current, there is a magnetic field.

In an ordinary room today, electric current is everywhere.

There are wires buried in the walls, and motors in refrigerators, washing machines, and air conditioners. When they are running with electricity, the power output changes all the time, which may affect the nearby magnetic field. According to SEER's standards, this is like setting up a magic formation inside your wall.

Things that are not plugged in are not honest either. Magnetic strips are embedded in the sealing strips of refrigerator doors, and permanent magnets are installed in motors, which still exist even when the device is turned off. Reinforced bars, iron pipes and other iron objects will also slightly deviate the direction of the earth's magnetic field nearby.
